grammar[0].fact: A deposit, *Pfand*, is 25 cents on most single-use bottles and cans, and 8 or 15 on reusable ones. The machine returns a slip for the till. So a homeless person sees a discarded can as a quarter of a euro, and Germans often leave bottles beside a bin for that reason.

document.intro: A real yellow sack, from Berlin. Germans really do read the bag. It lists what belongs inside, and the small line under the box says what does not. Yes, yoghurt pots are on it.
document.fact: The *Grüner Punkt*, the green dot on packaging, once meant the maker had paid towards recycling. Packaging has its own law now, and its own register. The rubbish has more paperwork than you do.

reading.intro: Maya has been found out. On her doormat is a clean, empty yoghurt pot and a note. She takes it to Frau Huber, who she thinks may have an idea who left it. Frau Huber has her glasses on already.
reading.fact: Germany recycles more than most, and the yellow bag or bin for packaging has been around since 1991. Each kind of waste has its own lorry and its own day, on a calendar on nearly every fridge. Deposit machines take back millions of bottles a day, and collecting them is a modest living for some.
